# [Agents]{.hidden} {.no-invert-dark-mode .center background-image="assets/robot-agent.jpg" background-size="cover" background-position="center"}

::: {.tc .white .pa1 .br3 .w-50 .absolute bottom="-5em" left=0 style="font-size: 3em; background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.8);"}
Agents
:::

## What's an agent?

::: incremental
* An LLM, in a harness, that calls tools repeatedly in a loop — deciding each next step from the last result

* Most agents have two kinds of tools: **read** tools to observe the world, and **write** tools to change it
:::

::: notes
This is Hadley Wickham's definition, from his "What is an agent?" post on Substack.

Simon Willison's shorter version: an LLM with a read tool and a write tool.

The "you know it when you see it" version: an autonomous system that needs minimal intervention to finish a task.

All three describe the same thing. The loop is what makes it an agent.
:::

## One tool call is not an agent {.center}

The quiz show called a tool. So why wasn't it an agent?

::: fragment
No loop, no decisions: the model called the sound tool and answered.
:::

::: notes
Recall the quiz show app: we registered one tool, and the model called it to play sounds during the game.

Each user message produced at most one tool call before the final answer.

An agent keeps calling tools in a loop, deciding each next step from the result of the last one.
:::

## The agent loop {.center}

::: incremental
* **Explore**: the agent reads to understand the world

* **Act**: the agent writes to change it

* **Observe**: the agent reads again to see what changed

* ...and repeat until the task is done
:::

::: notes
TODO: replace with an excalidraw diagram, in the style of the tools-how-it-works sequence in slides-07.

The loop is why agents feel different from a chat: the model, not the user, chooses the next step.

The harness (ellmer or chatlas) does the busy work: it runs each tool, sends the result back, and lets the model continue.
:::

## Read tools and write tools

| Read tools observe | Write tools change |
|:--------------------|:---------------------|
| Read a file | Write a file |
| List files | Edit a file |
| Search the codebase | Run a command |
| Look at data | Run code |

::: notes
Read and write is the smallest split that still makes an agent useful.

A coding agent is just an agent whose tools mirror how a human works on a codebase.

Hadley: "A coding agent is six functions in a trenchcoat" — read file, write file, edit file, list files, search, run command, plus a big system prompt of advice.
:::

# Your Turn `22_agent-1` {.slide-your-turn}

1. Your agent works in the Last Blockbuster's records folder.

1. Give it a **read** tool and a **write** tool, then ask it to build the win-back list.

1. Run the script it writes, then inspect the trace. Did it read the store rules before it wrote code?

{{< countdown 8:00 left=0 bottom="-2em" >}}

::: notes
The tool functions and the coding-agent system prompt are given.

Attendees document the tools, register them, and ask the agent to write `find_lapsed.R` or `find_lapsed.py`.

The attendee runs that script from inside `blockbuster/`.

Watch for the key choice: the agent writes a script instead of trying to read 1,500 rental rows through the tool.

Dry run in both R and Python: the trace reads `README.md`, then `policies.md`, then writes `find_lapsed.*`.
Both generated scripts produced 11 rows.
:::

## The manager finds another export {.center}

The first win-back list has 11 members.

::: notes
The agent has a working script, but it had to be told which files to read.

Next, the manager drops an old register export into the folder.

The agent needs a way to discover that file and make a narrow change to the script it already wrote.
:::

# Your Turn `23_agent-2` {.slide-your-turn}

1. Give your agent a **list files** tool and an **edit** tool.

1. Build the win-back list, then tell it the manager dropped an old register export in the folder. Do not name the file.

1. Run the patched script. The list drops from 11 members to 8.

{{< countdown 8:00 left=0 bottom="-2em" >}}

::: notes
`list_files` surfaces `rentals-old.csv` without the prompt naming it.

`edit_file` patches `find_lapsed.R` or `find_lapsed.py` instead of rewriting it.

A failed exact-match edit is a loud, safe error instead of a silent change.

The count changing from 11 to 8 makes the effect of the two new tools visible.

Dry run in both R and Python: the follow-up trace calls `list_files`, then patches `find_lapsed.*` with `edit_file`.
Both patched scripts produced eight rows without Greta Moss, Peter Ibarra, or Nora Ellis.
:::

## Should the agent run code? {.center}

You just played the run-code tool by hand.

Should the agent close that loop and repair its own errors?

::: notes
The upside is a closed loop and self-repair.

The risk is code with side effects against the store's data.

Ask the room what they would require first: a disposable copy, read-only data, dry-run flags, allow-listed commands, or approval prompts.
:::

## What counts as dangerous?

Danger = expensive, time-consuming, or impossible to **undo**

::: incremental
* Delete a file outside git

* Drop a database table

* Spend money

* Send an email

* Leak a secret or personal data
:::

::: notes
Hadley's framing from "Help! My coding agent can run code": dangerous means hard to undo.

Running the renewal script touches only a disposable, local fixture.

Sending a letter leaves the sandbox and reaches a real person.

The store's no-late-fees settlement is a reminder that careless promises have consequences.
:::

## Three ways to keep an agent in check

::: incremental
1. **Ask for permission** — but 99% of approvals are safe, so people click yes without reading

1. **Sandbox** — the OS constrains the process, but temp folders, package libraries, and network access all leak in

1. **Ask an LLM** — run in the sandbox, and when it rejects a call, have an LLM review the code and the conversation
:::

::: footer
[Help! My coding agent can run code](https://tidydesign.substack.com/p/help-my-coding-agent-can-run-code){preview-link=true}
:::

::: notes
The three approaches, in the order real tools adopted them.

Permission prompts become security theatre. Prefix allowlists fail: `git push` is safe, `git push --force` often isn't.

Sandboxing works but is fiddly: R needs a writable temp dir and a readable library path.

The state of the art is sandbox plus LLM review — which is what Posit Assistant does when it declines to run something risky. Some actions stay off-limits even when you ask for them explicitly.
:::

## Auto mode knows it's dangerous {.center}

> Running curl -fsSL ... | sh
>
> Sandboxed mktemp isn't writable. Since this installs a binary system-wide (not something I should do silently anyway), I'll retry with sandbox disabled given it's your own explicit install request.
>
> — Claude Code, asked to install air

::: notes
From Hadley's "Auto mode knows it's dangerous (and does it anyway)".

Both Claude Code and Codex recognized the curl-pipe-sh installer as dangerous and ran it anyway, because the user asked.

Best practice would be: download, read the script, then run. Neither agent read it.

Auto mode is less protective than it looks. Keep your own eyes on destructive steps.
:::

## Agents, recap

::: incremental
* An agent is an LLM, in a harness, calling tools in a loop

* Read tools observe; write tools change

* The harness does the busy work — you write the tools and the system prompt

* General tools make useful agents, and safety is the price
:::
